```text
   In the last chapter we covered how important it is to build habits that

how to set up systems to increase the likelihood that you’ll be able to in-

   It’s important to note that different people hope to get different
things out of playing poker. You have to decide what it is that you most
want to achieve when playing. Are you looking to win a little bit of extra
spending money like Adrienne “Talonchick” Rowesome discussed in the
inaugural episode of the podcast The Mindset Advantage? In that epi-
sode, she said that she started playing poker as a means to make a little
bit of extra fun money that she could spend on luxury items like designer
handbags. Her goals eventually changed as she became more successful
playing poker and it ultimately became her profession, but she started out
with a relatively modest aim.
```

```text
                                                     Systematizing Success

    Contrast this with the achievements of Brian Rast. He came on our
show to discuss his hopes for the super high roller event, which included
his plan to both satellite in and then win it outright. With skillful play and a
little bit of luck, he achieved both of those goals. We had him back to talk
about his process for maintaining his composure even when things
weren’t going so well! It was clear that he was focused and that his goals
were foremost in his mind during that particular event.
    Which camp are you in? Do you seek elite performance? Perhaps you
have your sights set on a World Series of Poker (WSOP) bracelet or a
World Poker Tour (WPT) title. Winning tons of money and gaining pres-
tige appeals to many players. Others are satisfied with pursuing poker as a
fun hobby for a little extra cash, and that’s perfectly acceptable, too.

Goals Versus Systems
Scott Adams wrote a delightful book called How to Fail at Almost Any-
thing and Still Win Big. You may know him as the creator of the comic
strip Dilbert. He has some pretty interesting ideas on how to create suc-
cess. In particular, he eschews ordinary goal setting for a process he calls
systems thinking. He says that “a goal is a specific objective that you ei-
ther achieve or don’t sometime in the future” (2013, p. 33). He goes on
to define a system as “something you do on a regular basis that increases
your odds of happiness in the future” (p. 33). Therefore, if you do some-
thing every day, it’s a system. He states emphatically that “goal-oriented
people exist in a state of continuous presuccess failure at best, and per-
manent failure at worst if things never work out.” Systems people, on the
other hand, are successful every time they apply their systems. He argues
that if we stay in a constant state of failure, we are bound to feel discour-
aged, which makes us more likely to quit on our goals. By his way of
thinking, your goal is to design and implement a set of systems for your-
self that will inevitably lead to your success. I’ll have a lot more on this
topic, later in the chapter. For now, take some time to think about how
this idea could work for you.
   Stephen Guise discusses the same concept in his book Mini Habits. He
```

```text
Peak Poker Performance

says that it’s more mentally energy efficient to break things down into
small components that are easily digested. Such an approach also has the
benefit of being inherently less stressful. Imagine that you have a goal of
losing 100 pounds and after one year you have lost 50 pounds. Losing
that much weight is a real accomplishment, but because it falls short of
the overall goal, it is typically seen as a failure. Besides that, when you
have a large goal, each small step along the way feels as if it contributes
almost nothing. This all adds up to a de-motivating experience! The solu-
tion is to develop a system so that you can feel successful each day you
work on or accomplish a component of it.
    He says we should create tiny systems out of our goals and action
plans and that by doing so we will increase our levels of happiness and the
likelihood of success. He says that tiny systems are more effective for
two reasons:

     ♠ Big intentions aren’t worth much if they don’t bring us results; you
        might intend to study poker for two hours a day, but if you don’t
        actually do that, your intention isn’t worth much.
     ♠ We tend to over-estimate our self-control. We think we can force
        ourselves to do things, but in reality self-control is quite limited.


    You add these two factors together and you can see that there is a
mismatch between desire and reality. Guise suggests that the solution is
to go absurdly small with your systems. He says that if you want to start
exercising, implement a system of one push-up a day. This may seem silly,
but what generally happens is that after you do one, you’ll probably be
inspired to do more. Even if you don’t, you’ll still have achieved your
benchmark for the day.
    A major reason why a small system like this can work is because it gets
past the brain, natural resistance centers. Our brain has evolved to resist
change and this is a way to short circuit that tendency. Second, enacting
a tiny system helps you develop a routine. Routines build up neural net-
works in the brain, which make them run on autopilot. No thought is re-
```

```text
                                                   Systematizing Success

quired. Once the cue is present, the routine is triggered.
   Virtually all successful poker players follow certain routines and are
pretty rigid in their adherence to their systems. They have specific activi-
ties that they do either every day or almost every day in pursuit of their
goals. I believe this is how certain players achieve so much success. If you
can figure out your personal success systems and then apply them every
single day, you will increase your chances of success.

Systematize Your Process
University of Alabama football coach Nick Saban tells his players not to fo-
cus on winning; instead they are instructed to focus on what he calls the
process. This is Saban’s philosophy, which is rooted in cognitive behavioral
psychology. If you play for him, you’ll quickly learn to focus on the here and
now. If you are overly concerned about the future or stuck in the past,
you’ll miss what’s going on right now and that’s not good for your game.
   Saban also teaches that it is detrimental to focus on outcomes. If you
are attached to the outcome of a game, you have already lost. He teaches
his players to focus on each play as though it was a game in and of itself.
You can do the same thing at the poker table. Look at each hand you play
as a game within a game. Your goal is to play it as well as you can without
regard to the outcome.
   Saban talks about adversity, too. He says that adversity is your friend.
Achieving your goals in spite of adversity is that much sweeter. Also,
mental toughness and diversity are prerequisites for dealing with adver-
sity effectively.
   While Saban’s bigger goal is to win championships, he has his players
focus on the little things that will add up over time. You can do the same
thing. Think about the small things you can do every day that will change
your poker trajectory for the better.
   We can’t leave this section without including some wisdom from John
Wooden. He is considered by many to be the greatest college basketball
coach of all time, and he was notorious for having his players focus on the
fundamentals. There are some nuggets of wisdom in his philosophy that
```

```text
Peak Poker Performance

can surely be applied to poker. Andrew Hill, who played for Wooden, said
that he never emphasized winning. Instead he instructed his team to play
their hardest. He told his players that he would rather that they play their
best and lose than win by playing a mediocre game. According to
Wooden, if you won, but didn’t play your best, then you didn’t really win.
If you lost, but you played your best, then you didn’t really lose. Wooden
said, “Never mention winning. My idea is that you can lose when you out-
score somebody in a game, and you can win when you’re outscored.”
    Jack Ramsay, a broadcaster and basketball coach, said of Wooden, “His
attention to detail created routines that we all learned and adopted. Every
day at practice, we did the things that he preached – running, balance,
change of direction, ball handling, just about every fundamental facet of
the game, about seven, eight minutes every single day.”
    How much effort are you putting into your fundamentals? Are you
proud of the game you are showing up with most often? If not, remember
Wooden’s primary suggestion, which was that you should try your hardest
to improve a little bit each day and make every practice a masterpiece.

Create Perfect Days
Hal Elrod is a guy who has experienced some adversity in his life. At just
20 years old he was hit head on by a drunk driver and was dead for sev-
eral minutes. After he was revived, he spent several days in a coma. Once
he fully recovered he decided to devote his life to helping others over-
come adversity. He has written a couple of books. The one most relevant
to setting up success routines is called The Miracle Morning (2014), in
which he advises that it is possible to take our lives to the next level by
implementing a morning routine:

      How you wake up each day and your morning routine (or lack
      thereof) dramatically affects your levels of success in every
      single area of your life... focused, productive, successful
      mornings generate focused, productive, successful days –
      which inevitably create a successful life.
```

```text
                                                  Systematizing Success

   Likewise, Elrod implies that if you start off the day in an unfocused
way, it will generally lead to an unfocused, unproductive mediocre day.
   How do you start your days out? Have you noticed whether or not
your game is affected if you get off to a poor start in the morning? Could
you set up your days in such a way that it is easier to play your A game
more consistently? Elrod says that we must prioritize and devote time to
our personal development each and every day if we want to improve our
odds of success in any endeavor. He specifically prescribes six daily prac-
tices that have been shown to improve overall mindset when they are
used systematically. He believes that if we want to be successful, we
should start each day with:

   ♠ silence
   ♠ affirmations
   ♠ visualization
   ♠ exercise
   ♠ reading
   ♠ scribing.

Silence
Elrod argues that we need to start each day with a period of calm, silent
reflection about what is most important for us to focus on for the day.
Whether you start the day off with prayer, mindfulness, or meditation,
know that there is a wide body of scientific research that indicates that
these practices reduce stress, increase clarity, and improve focus.
    Here’s a quick one-minute meditation you can make a tiny habit out of,
if you wish. Sit comfortably with your spine straight. Keep your feet on
the ground. Jon Kabat-Zinn, a well-known meditation teacher, recom-
mends sitting with dignity. With your hands in your lap, gently close your
eyes. Take a deep breath and notice your breath as it travels in through
your nose and down into your lungs. Continue paying attention as you ex-
```

```text
Peak Poker Performance

hale. Simply keep focused on each breath as you inhale and exhale – until
your mind wanders, as it invariably will. When that happens, just bring
your awareness back to your breathing. Repeat this process for one min-
ute or five. You can do more if you like. The idea is to get into the routine
of it. Small amounts of focused meditation over a regular period of time
show tremendous neurologic benefit.

Affirmations
Next up, affirmations can be used to reprogram your mind. Elrod suggests
that we write down our affirmations, which are really just Westernized
versions of mantras. The word mantra by the way is Sanskrit for “tools of
the mind.” When you practice using affirmations, you are literally creating
tools for your mind. Elrod says that when we repeatedly tell ourselves
who we want to be and what we want to accomplish, these affirmations
are imprinted on our minds. The idea is that you write out some state-
ments that you want to affirm to yourself and read over them a few
times each day.

Visualization
To take this even further, you can use visualization, where you imagine in
vivid detail the specific behaviors you would like to enact or situations you
would like to respond to optimally. Visualization literally “primes” you for
the activities that lie ahead. Athletes frequently use visualization to en-
hance their performance and there is no reason that poker players cannot
use it, too. You can imagine yourself successfully dealing with bad beats.
Visualization is a great strategy to use to prepare yourself for dealing with
obnoxious people effectively. You can even visualize yourself studying,
working out, or really anything else that you want to accomplish. Elrod
suggests mentally rehearsing what you will do specifically to achieve the
outcomes you desire.
   Here’s a sample visualization to get you started. Close your eyes and
take a deep breath and exhale gently. Imagine that it is sometime in the
future. It is the moment when you have achieved some long awaited
```

```text
                                                   Systematizing Success

poker goal that you have set for yourself. Perhaps it is winning a major
event like a WPT Championship or a WSOP bracelet. Develop an image in
your mind of the goal you are striving for and the day it becomes a reality.
    As you imagine yourself in this setting, having already achieved your
goal, imagine the expression on your face. Perhaps it’s an ear-to-ear grin.
Or maybe you are the calm, relaxed picture of contentment. Spend a
moment sitting with that image.
    Next, notice your posture. Is there an air of confidence to your physical
presence? Are you standing tall? How is your breathing? What are you
thinking about now that you have achieved your goal, now that your
dream has become a reality? How is everyone around you acting? How
does your achievement make your friends and family feel? Experience
their words of encouragement and the pats on the back you receive.
    As you enjoy the rewards of your accomplishment, ask yourself, “Was
it worth it? Was it worth all of the dedication and commitment that it
took to get here?” And as you conclude that it was, start going back in
time.
    Notice some of the obstacles you had to overcome along the way to
achieve your goal. Remember the negative people with whom you had to
contend. Maybe they told you that you weren’t capable of reaching such
an achievement. Think about some of your beliefs that you had to change
about your capabilities. Pay attention to how serious you became about
your goal. When was the moment when you became totally committed to
reaching your goal?
    Continue back in time and reflect on your journey. Perhaps it’s taken
months or even years to get where you are now. Notice how far you have
come. Allow yourself to experience satisfaction over what you have ac-
complished. Before you open your eyes, feel good about allowing your
mind and your emotions to work in harmony.
    As you can see, you can put yourself in the future using the power of
your imagination. Doing this has a couple of benefits: imagining success
can be motivating, and taking some time to think about obstacles can
help us plan for them in advance.
```
